Rewrite the following essay substantively. Aim for 1500 words; the acceptable range is 1200-1500 words, and the corpus-wide hard range is 800-1500 words. Use at least 6 natural paragraphs, preferably approximately 10 paragraphs. Do not include a heading.

SOURCE ESSAY:
Some time ago I wrote in these columns an article called “The Extraordinary Cabman.” I am now in a position to contribute my experience of a still more extraordinary cab. The extraordinary thing about the cab was that it did not like me; it threw me out violently in the middle of the Strand. If my friends who read the DAILY NEWS are as romantic (and as rich) as I take them to be, I presume that this experience is not uncommon. I suppose that they are all being thrown out of cabs, all over London. Still, as there are some people, virginal and remote from the world, who have not yet had this luxurious experience, I will give a short account of the psychology of myself when my hansom cab ran into the side of a motor omnibus, and I hope hurt it.

I do not need to dwell on the essential romance of the hansom cab—that one really noble modern thing which our age, when it is judged, will gravely put beside the Parthenon. It is really modern in that it is both secret and swift. My particular hansom cab was modern in these two respects; it was also very modern in the fact that it came to grief. But it is also English; it is not to be found abroad; it belongs to a beautiful, romantic country where nearly everybody is pretending to be richer than they are, and acting as if they were. It is comfortable, and yet it is reckless; and that combination is the very soul of England. But although I had always realised all these good qualities in a hansom cab, I had not experienced all the possibilities, or, as the moderns put it, all the aspects of that vehicle. My enunciation of the merits of a hansom cab had been always made when it was the right way up. Let me, therefore, explain how I felt when I fell out of a hansom cab for the first and, I am happy to believe, the last time. Polycrates threw one ring into the sea to propitiate the Fates. I have thrown one hansom cab into the sea (if you will excuse a rather violent metaphor) and the Fates are, I am quite sure, propitiated. Though I am told they do not like to be told so.

I was driving yesterday afternoon in a hansom cab down one of the sloping streets into the Strand, reading one of my own admirable articles with continual pleasure, and still more continual surprise, when the horse fell forward, scrambled a moment on the scraping stones, staggered to his feet again, and went forward. The horses in my cabs often do this, and I have learnt to enjoy my own articles at any angle of the vehicle. So I did not see anything at all odd about the way the horse went on again. But I saw it suddenly in the faces of all the people on the pavement. They were all turned towards me, and they were all struck with fear suddenly, as with a white flame out of the sky. And one man half ran out into the road with a movement of the elbow as if warding off a blow, and tried to stop the horse. Then I knew that the reins were lost, and the next moment the horse was like a living thunder-bolt. I try to describe things exactly as they seemed to me; many details I may have missed or mis-stated; many details may have, so to speak, gone mad in the race down the road. I remember that I once called one of my experiences narrated in this paper “A Fragment of Fact.” This is, at any rate, a fragment of fact. No fact could possibly be more fragmentary than the sort of fact that I expected to be at the bottom of that street.

.....

I believe in preaching to the converted; for I have generally found that the converted do not understand their own religion. Thus I have always urged in this paper that democracy has a deeper meaning than democrats understand; that is, that common and popular things, proverbs, and ordinary sayings always have something in them unrealised by most who repeat them. Here is one. We have all heard about the man who is in momentary danger, and who sees the whole of his life pass before him in a moment. In the cold, literal, and common sense of words, this is obviously a thundering lie. Nobody can pretend that in an accident or a mortal crisis he elaborately remembered all the tickets he had ever taken to Wimbledon, or all the times that he had ever passed the brown bread and butter.

But in those few moments, while my cab was tearing towards the traffic of the Strand, I discovered that there is a truth behind this phrase, as there is behind all popular phrases. I did really have, in that short and shrieking period, a rapid succession of a number of fundamental points of view. I had, so to speak, about five religions in almost as many seconds. My first religion was pure Paganism, which among sincere men is more shortly described as extreme fear. Then there succeeded a state of mind which is quite real, but for which no proper name has ever been found. The ancients called it Stoicism, and I think it must be what some German lunatics mean (if they mean anything) when they talk about Pessimism. It was an empty and open acceptance of the thing that happens—as if one had got beyond the value of it. And then, curiously enough, came a very strong contrary feeling—that things mattered very much indeed, and yet that they were something more than tragic. It was a feeling, not that life was unimportant, but that life was much too important ever to be anything but life. I hope that this was Christianity. At any rate, it occurred at the moment when we went crash into the omnibus.

It seemed to me that the hansom cab simply turned over on top of me, like an enormous hood or hat. I then found myself crawling out from underneath it in attitudes so undignified that they must have added enormously to that great cause to which the Anti-Puritan League and I have recently dedicated ourselves. I mean the cause of the pleasures of the people. As to my demeanour when I emerged, I have two confessions to make, and they are both made merely in the interests of mental science. The first is that whereas I had been in a quite pious frame of mind the moment before the collision, when I got to my feet and found I had got off with a cut or two I began (like St. Peter) to curse and to swear. A man offered me a newspaper or something that I had dropped. I can distinctly remember consigning the paper to a state of irremediable spiritual ruin. I am very sorry for this now, and I apologise both to the man and to the paper. I have not the least idea what was the meaning of this unnatural anger; I mention it as a psychological confession. It was immediately followed by extreme hilarity, and I made so many silly jokes to the policeman that he disgraced himself by continual laughter before all the little boys in the street, who had hitherto taken him seriously.

.....

There is one other odd thing about the matter which I also mention as a curiosity of the human brain or deficiency of brain. At intervals of about every three minutes I kept on reminding the policeman that I had not paid the cabman, and that I hoped he would not lose his money. He said it would be all right, and the man would appear. But it was not until about half an hour afterwards that it suddenly struck me with a shock intolerable that the man might conceivably have lost more than half a crown; that he had been in danger as well as I. I had instinctively regarded the cabman as something uplifted above accidents, a god. I immediately made inquiries, and I am happy to say that they seemed to have been unnecessary.

But henceforward I shall always understand with a darker and more delicate charity those who take tythe of mint, and anise, and cumin, and neglect the weightier matters of the law; I shall remember how I was once really tortured with owing half a crown to a man who might have been dead. Some admirable men in white coats at the Charing Cross Hospital tied up my small injury, and I went out again into the Strand. I felt upon me even a kind of unnatural youth; I hungered for something untried. So to open a new chapter in my life I got into a hansom cab.

message.content:
Not long ago, I shared a piece titled "The Extraordinary Cabman" in these pages. Today, I have the opportunity to recount an even more remarkable experience involving a cab. What made this cab so extraordinary was its distinct aversion to me; it ejected me forcefully right in the middle of the Strand. If my esteemed readers of the DAILY NEWS possess the romantic spirit (and wealth) that I assume they do, then I suspect this is an experience that is not entirely rare. It stands to reason that many of them may have also found themselves unceremoniously tossed from cabs across London. Yet, for the sake of those few who remain untouched by this particular luxury, I will describe the psychological journey I underwent when my hansom cab collided with a motor omnibus, leaving me to wonder about the fate of my dignity.

The innate charm of the hansom cab is something I need not elaborate on—the quintessential modern creation that, when our era is reflected upon, will be regarded alongside the grandeur of the Parthenon. It embodies modernity in its swiftness and secrecy. My particular hansom cab exemplified these traits, though it met with unfortunate circumstances as well. It is a uniquely English invention, absent in foreign lands, rooted in a beautiful and romantic country where most inhabitants pretend to possess wealth beyond their means. The hansom is both comfortable and reckless, and this juxtaposition encapsulates the very essence of England. Despite my appreciation for the many virtues of a hansom cab, I had yet to confront its full spectrum of possibilities—or, as contemporary expressions go, its various aspects. My previous assertions regarding the merits of such vehicles were made while they were upright. Therefore, allow me to convey my feelings during that fateful moment when I was unceremoniously ejected from a hansom cab for what I hope is the first and last time. While Polycrates tossed one of his rings into the sea to appease the Fates, I have metaphorically cast a hansom cab into the depths, and I trust the Fates are satisfied, even if they do not appreciate being told so.

Yesterday afternoon, I found myself riding in a hansom cab, descending one of the gentle inclines toward the Strand, engrossed in the pleasure and surprise of reading one of my own commendable articles. Suddenly, the horse faltered, stumbled briefly on the rough stones, and then regained its footing. This was a common occurrence for the horses in my cabs, and I had grown accustomed to enjoying my articles regardless of the vehicle's angle. Thus, I thought nothing of the horse's momentary struggle. However, a glance at the faces of the pedestrians revealed a stark change; they were transfixed with fear, as if struck by a bolt of lightning. One man even rushed into the street, his arm raised as if to deflect an impending blow, attempting to halt the horse's advance. It was then I understood that the reins had slipped from my grasp, and in an instant, the horse surged forward like a bolt of lightning. I strive to recount events as they appeared to me, acknowledging that I may have overlooked or misstated numerous details, and that many aspects might have been distorted in the chaos of that wild dash down the street. I once referred to a past experience as “A Fragment of Fact”; this moment, too, qualifies as a fragment of reality, though it is one that I could never have anticipated at the street's end.

I am a firm believer in addressing those who already hold certain convictions, for I have often found that they do not fully grasp the depth of their own beliefs. This has led me to assert that democracy encompasses a meaning that often eludes those who champion it. Ordinary expressions, proverbs, and common phrases frequently harbor insights that many who repeat them fail to recognize. Take, for instance, the notion that a person in imminent danger can witness their entire life flash before their eyes in an instant. In the stark, literal sense, this is an outright fabrication. No one can claim that during a crisis, they meticulously recalled every event, every ticket they ever purchased to Wimbledon, or the countless times they shared brown bread and butter.

Yet, as my cab hurtled toward the bustling traffic of the Strand, I discovered that there is indeed a kernel of truth nestled within that phrase, as is often the case with popular expressions. In those fleeting, shrill moments, I experienced a rapid succession of fundamental perspectives. I went through what might be described as five distinct religions in the span of just a few seconds. Initially, I found myself engulfed in pure Paganism, better known among sincere individuals as sheer terror. This state was soon succeeded by a mindset that, while real, defies proper nomenclature. The ancients might have referred to it as Stoicism, and perhaps it aligns with what some German philosophers mean when they discuss Pessimism. It was an empty acceptance of whatever fate had in store, as if I had transcended the significance of it all. Strangely, this was followed by an intense contrary feeling—that life mattered immensely, and yet it was something beyond mere tragedy. I sensed that life was far too vital to ever be reduced to anything less than life itself. I hope this realization was a reflection of Christianity; at least, it coincided with the moment of our collision with the omnibus.

In what felt like a surreal twist, the hansom cab seemed to topple over me, enveloping me like a massive hood. I soon found myself crawling out from beneath it, in such undignified postures that I must have inadvertently contributed significantly to the cause championed by the Anti-Puritan League, with which I recently aligned myself—namely, the pursuit of the people’s pleasures. Regarding my demeanor upon emerging from beneath the cab, I must confess two things, both shared solely for the sake of psychological inquiry. First, just moments before the collision, I had been in a seemingly serene state of mind; however, upon standing up and realizing I had sustained only minor cuts, I began, much like St. Peter, to unleash a torrent of curses. A man approached, offering me a newspaper or some item I had dropped. I can vividly recall condemning that paper to a fate of irredeemable spiritual ruin. I now deeply regret this outburst, and I extend my apologies to both the man and the newspaper. The reason for this inexplicable anger escapes me, but I mention it as a psychological curiosity. This outburst was swiftly followed by a wave of hilarity; I made so many absurd jokes to the policeman that he succumbed to laughter, much to the chagrin of the little boys in the street who had previously taken him seriously.

There was another peculiar aspect of this incident that I mention as an intriguing facet of human psychology—or perhaps a deficiency thereof. Every three minutes or so, I found myself reminding the policeman that I had yet to pay the cabman and fervently hoped he would not suffer a financial loss. The officer reassured me that everything would be fine and that the cabman would show up. However, it wasn’t until half an hour later that it struck me with a jolt that the cabman might have been at risk of losing more than just a small fare; he had faced danger alongside me. In my mind, I had instinctively elevated the cabman to a status akin to that of a deity, impervious to mishaps. I promptly began to make inquiries and was relieved to learn that my concerns had been unfounded.

From that moment on, I gained a deeper and more nuanced understanding of those who meticulously adhere to the lesser details while neglecting the more significant matters at hand; I, too, felt the weight of guilt for having owed a mere half-crown to a person who might have been injured or worse. Some dedicated gentlemen in white coats at Charing Cross Hospital attended to my minor injuries, after which I stepped back out into the bustling Strand. A sense of unnatural youth enveloped me, igniting a yearning for uncharted experiences. Thus, to mark the start of a new chapter in my life, I climbed into yet another hansom cab.
